claim: NJ cooling rule is two-stage and time-boxed: 135 F to 70 F within 2 hours, then to refrigeration temperature within a total of 4 hours (N.J.A.C. 8:24-3.5(d)).
problem: Misstated legal rule. N.J.A.C. 8:24-3.5(d)1 reads: 'i. Within two hours, from 135 degrees Fahrenheit to 70 degrees Fahrenheit; and ii. Within four hours, from 70 degrees Fahrenheit to refrigeration temperatures.' The second stage is four hours FROM 70 F, i.e. up to six hours total - not 'a total of 4 hours'. 'Total of 4 hours' is the wording of other jurisdictions' codes, not this one.
fix: Rewrite as '135 F to 70 F within 2 hours, then 70 F to 41 F within 4 more hours (up to 6 hours total)', quote 8:24-3.5(d)1.i and ii verbatim, and align the alert/degree-minute thresholds and any customer-facing comparison table to the 6-hour total.

claim: Standard business owner policies exclude spoilage from mechanical/refrigeration breakdown by default; coverage requires a spoilage endorsement or equipment-breakdown extension, often capped around $10,000.
problem: Two problems with the cited Insureon page. (1) 'Often capped around $10,000' appears nowhere on the page - the figure is unsourced. (2) The page states the opposite of the 'equipment-breakdown extension' framing: equipment breakdown coverage 'will pay to repair or replace the equipment that malfunctioned, but it will not cover the cost of spoiled inventory'; only a spoilage endorsement / utility service interruption endorsement covers lost perishables.
fix: Delete the $10,000 cap or replace it with a sourced figure from a carrier/broker page that states a limit. Reword to 'commercial property policies usually need a spoilage (or utility service interruption) endorsement; equipment breakdown coverage by itself repairs the box, not the inventory', and keep the caveat that these are broker summaries.

claim: USDA ERS supermarket shrink estimates put retail loss at 11.4% for fresh fruit and 9.7% for fresh vegetables (2005-06 data)... ERS publications 2015 and 2019, source_url chartId=92910.
problem: The numbers are real but the citation does not support them. The cited Charts of Note page (4/23/2019) covers only the 2011-12 data (2,900 stores; 4.1% bananas to 43.1% papayas) and contains no 11.4%/9.7% figures. Those figures come from ERS Economic Information Bulletin No. 44, March 2009 ('annual supermarket losses for 2005 and 2006 averaged 11.4 percent for fresh fruit, 9.7 percent for fresh vegetables, and 4.5 percent for fresh meat, poultry, and seafood'). No 2015 ERS publication was found carrying them.
fix: Split the entry into two citations - the 2009 EIB-44 report summary for 11.4%/9.7% (https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/44306/10894_eib44_reportsummary.pdf) and the chartId=92910 page for the 2011-12 4.1%-43.1% range - and correct the year label to '2005-06 data, ERS EIB-44 (2009); 2011-12 data, ERS charts of note (2019)'.

claim: SmartSense by Digi pricing: a public school-district bid shows ~$175/sensor, ~$400/gateway per site, ~$25/site/year monitoring (source_url smartsense.co/food-service).
problem: The cited page contains no pricing at all (it is a marketing page that does name Wegmans, sweetgreen, Cafe Rio and honeygrow as customers, which is confirmed). The bid-derived prices are unattributed in the brief, so a reader cannot check them; the figures do appear in third-party district documents found by search but not at the cited URL.
fix: Add the actual bid/proposal document URL that lists ~$175 per display sensor, ~$400 per gateway, and $25/site/year, and label these as 'one district's proposal pricing, not a list price'. Keep smartsense.co/food-service for the customer-name claim only.

claim: Reported single-incident losses: ... a Chicago restaurant reported nearly $20,000 of loss from back-to-back equipment failures (2026 press release).
problem: No source_url is given for this number (the entry's source_url is the Lincoln, NE article only). Independently, the underlying July 2026 press release (Smack Dab, Rogers Park) reports about $19,500 total impact, of which food spoilage was only roughly $2,000-$3,000; the rest is a convection-oven replacement and lost revenue. Presenting it as a refrigeration/spoilage loss overstates the spoilage figure.
fix: Give the press release URL, and restate as 'about $19,500 total impact, of which roughly $2-3k was spoiled cooler product' - or drop the incident, since the Lincoln, NE $1,800 case is cleaner.

claim: Monnit ALTA standard temperature sensor: $116 each; probe add-ons $24-$117; NIST certification +$71.
problem: The $116 sensor and the $71 NIST upcharge are exactly right, but the probe add-on range is wrong at the low end: the Monnit product page lists a 3-foot probe at +$11, then $24 (5 ft), $31, $35, $62 and $117 (100 ft). The stated range starts at $24.
fix: Change to 'probe add-ons +$11 to +$117 depending on lead length'.

claim: Open-source stack parts cost: $15-$25 in parts per cooler (ESP32 $8-$12, waterproof DS18B20 $3-$6, reed switch, resistor).
problem: Could not be verified: the cited guide (imakethings.fyi) returned HTTP 403 on every attempt, so neither the $15-$25 total nor the component prices are checkable from the cited source. This price also drives the pilot budget and the 'commodity hardware' risk, so it is load-bearing.
fix: Replace with an openable source (e.g. an ESP32 and DS18B20 product page or an accessible build guide) and cite component prices individually, or mark the figure explicitly as an estimate (inference) rather than a sourced price.

claim: Sensaphone Sentinel SCD-1200 roughly $553-$800 depending on reseller; WEB600 about $392 (source_url absoluteautomation.com collection page).
problem: The cited collection page renders no prices (only a shipping/returns banner), so the range is unsupported at the cited URL. Reseller listings found by search put SCD-1200 at about $553.50-$615 and WEB600 at about $391.50-$435; the $800 top of the range was not found anywhere.
fix: Cite a live product page with a price, narrow the range to what a reseller actually lists (e.g. 'about $554-$615'), and note that cellular variants are much higher (~$1,560).

claim: ThermoWorks ThermaData WiFi: $205 (ambient) to $335 (removable external probe); thermocouple versions $289.
problem: The cited ambient product page confirms $205.00, 18,000 readings and an included NIST-traceable calibration certificate, but contains none of the probe or thermocouple prices, so most of the stated range is uncited.
fix: Cite the probe and thermocouple product pages separately for $335 and $289, or state only the verified $205 ambient price and label the rest as unverified.

claim: Roughly 1,650 restaurant/bar establishments in Middlesex County alone per Census CBP figures (fit_score rationale).
problem: Not verified from a primary source (Census API requires a key, and the brief admits the count came from secondary aggregations). A secondary CBP-derived figure found in verification is 1,746 NAICS 722 establishments for 2022, about 6% higher; 'roughly 1,650' is not wrong by much but is not a number the orchestrator can quote.
fix: Either state 'approximately 1,700-1,750 paid-employee food service establishments (CBP 2022, via secondary analysis)' with the secondary URL, or drop the figure and say 'well over 1,000' pending a direct CBP pull.

claim: 'Does the food code require automated logs? ... confirmed: true' (a negative finding: no NJ provision mandating a log format or cadence).
problem: The substance is honest and correctly cautious, but marking an absence-of-rule finding as 'confirmed: true' overstates it - the source (8:24-2.1) shows the person in charge must supervise routine monitoring and have scaled/calibrated thermometers, which is not the same as a searched-and-verified absence across Chapter 24.
fix: Set confirmed to false (or add a 'nature: negative finding' field) and say 'no provision found in the subchapters reviewed; absence not exhaustively verified'.

claim: fit_score: demand 15, local_buyers 13, ability_to_pay 9, technical_feasibility 19, legal_risk_low 12, defensibility 7, total 75.
problem: Arithmetic is correct (sums to 75) and the direction of each sub-score is consistent with the evidence, but the brief never states the scale/maximum for sub-scores, so 'within range' cannot be audited, and legal_risk_low = 12 reads low against a rationale that calls legal risk 'genuinely low' (12 is 60% on a /20 scale).
fix: State the scale explicitly (e.g. each sub-score 0-20, total /120) and either raise legal_risk_low to match 'genuinely low' or qualify the rationale ('low on audio/face-recognition risk, medium on unsettled employee-monitoring questions').
